chapter.name: Fundamental Rights: Your Claim Against the State
chapter.blurb: The idea and list of fundamental rights, equality, freedoms, rights against exploitation and of religion, constitutional remedies, and the limits and amendment of rights.

concepts.name: What fundamental rights are
concepts.description: The idea of enforceable rights against the State, where they sit in the Constitution and how a law that breaks them is treated.
concepts.idea: Fundamental rights are guarantees in Part III that a citizen can enforce in court against the State.
concepts.rule: Part III of the Constitution (Articles 12 to 35) lists the fundamental rights. Article 12 says who counts as 'the State': the Union and State governments, Parliament and the legislatures, and local and other authorities. Article 13 makes any law that takes away or waters down these rights void to that extent. The rights are justiciable, so a person whose right is violated can go straight to the Supreme Court under Article 32. They are not absolute: the State may impose reasonable restrictions in the public interest. The right to property was removed from this list by the 44th Amendment (1978) and now survives as an ordinary legal right in Article 300A.
concepts.example: A person whose house is demolished by a municipal body without notice can question the action as an act of 'the State'.

concepts.name: Equality before the law
concepts.description: Articles 14 to 18: equal protection, no discrimination, equal opportunity in public jobs, ending untouchability and titles.
concepts.idea: The State must treat people alike and cannot use birth or status to give some people advantage.
concepts.rule: Article 14 promises equality before the law and equal protection of the laws. Article 15 forbids discrimination on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth, though special provisions for women, children and weaker sections are allowed. Article 16 guarantees equality of opportunity in public employment, with provision for reservation. Article 17 abolishes untouchability and makes its practice punishable. Article 18 abolishes titles, except military and academic distinctions, and stops a citizen from accepting titles from a foreign State.
concepts.example: A government job advertisement cannot be limited to men of one caste without a permitted reason.

concepts.name: Freedoms and protection of life and liberty
concepts.description: Articles 19 to 22: the six freedoms, safeguards for accused persons, the right to life and personal liberty, education and arrest.
concepts.idea: Citizens enjoy specific freedoms, and life, liberty and fair procedure are protected against arbitrary State action.
concepts.rule: Article 19(1) gives citizens six freedoms: speech and expression; assembling peaceably without arms; forming associations, unions or cooperative societies; moving freely throughout India; residing and settling in any part; and practising any profession or carrying on any trade. Each can be limited by reasonable restrictions. Article 20 protects an accused against a law applied backwards, against being punished twice for the same offence and against being forced to testify against oneself. Article 21 says no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except by procedure established by law. Article 21A (86th Amendment, 2002) makes education free and compulsory for children aged 6 to 14. Article 22 gives safeguards on arrest, including being told the grounds and being produced before a magistrate within 24 hours.
concepts.example: A person arrested must be taken before a magistrate within 24 hours, excluding travel time.

concepts.name: Rights against exploitation, of religion and of minorities
concepts.description: Articles 23 to 30: bans on forced labour and child labour, freedom of religion, and cultural and educational rights.
concepts.idea: Articles 23 to 30 protect people from exploitation and protect religious and cultural freedoms.
concepts.rule: Article 23 prohibits human trafficking and forced labour (begar). Article 24 forbids employing children below 14 in factories, mines or other hazardous work. Article 25 gives every person freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion, subject to public order, morality and health. Article 26 lets religious denominations manage their own religious affairs. Article 27 says no one can be compelled to pay taxes for promoting a particular religion. Article 28 restricts religious instruction in institutions wholly maintained by the State. Article 29 protects the language, script and culture of any section of citizens, and Article 30 gives religious and linguistic minorities the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.
concepts.example: A factory cannot employ a 12-year-old to work on hazardous machinery.

concepts.name: Constitutional remedies and writs
concepts.description: Article 32, Article 226, the five writs and the special status of the right to move the courts.
concepts.idea: Article 32 makes the right to move the Supreme Court a fundamental right, and the courts issue writs to enforce rights.
concepts.rule: Article 32 lets a person go directly to the Supreme Court to enforce a fundamental right, and Dr Ambedkar called it the heart and soul of the Constitution. High Courts have a similar and wider power under Article 226, which can also be used for purposes other than fundamental rights. The five writs are habeas corpus (produce the person detained), mandamus (a command to perform a public duty), prohibition (stops a lower court from exceeding jurisdiction), certiorari (quashes an order of a lower court or tribunal) and quo warranto (asks by what authority a person holds a public office). Parliament can make the right to move the courts unavailable only as the Constitution provides, such as during a national emergency under Article 359.
concepts.example: A writ of habeas corpus can be filed if a person is held without lawful authority.

concepts.name: Limits, emergencies and landmark ideas about rights
concepts.description: Reasonable restrictions, armed forces, the effect of an emergency, the amendment power and the basic structure idea.
concepts.idea: Rights can be limited and amended, but the Supreme Court has held that the basic structure cannot be destroyed.
concepts.rule: Rights come with reasonable restrictions. Article 33 lets Parliament modify these rights for members of the armed forces and similar services. During a national emergency the rights under Article 19 are suspended when the emergency is declared on the ground of war or external aggression, and the President can suspend the right to move the courts for the enforcement of other rights under Article 359; after the 44th Amendment the rights under Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended. Article 368 gives Parliament the power to amend the Constitution. In Golaknath (1967) the Supreme Court held that Parliament could not amend fundamental rights, but in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) it held that Parliament can amend the Constitution but cannot change its basic structure.
concepts.example: Article 21 remains available even during an emergency.
